title: A Thousand Heads
hook: a person with a thousand heads who is all this and still more: the Veda's first picture of god in everything
carry: god is in all this, every face included
tomorrow: if god is everything, is everything all of god?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nasadiya Sukta ended: the one in highest heaven surely knows, or perhaps does not know.

A festival crowd, photographed from a rooftop. At first it looks like one moving surface. Then you zoom in. Heads, thousands of them. Hands in the air. Sandals, a child on someone's shoulders. One crowd, and countless people, and you can't quite say where one ends and the next begins. The Rig Veda has a hymn that opens on a picture like that, except the crowd is one person, and the person is bigger than the world. After a hymn that asked who knows, here's one that begins by describing.
screen: `A CROWD FROM A ROOFTOP.` → `ONE THING, COUNTLESS PEOPLE.` → `NOW MAKE IT ONE PERSON.`

segments.voice: Purusha means person. Here, in the Rig Veda, it names a cosmic person, and the hymn opens: sahasra-shirsha purushah. The Purusha has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet. Many readers hear thousand as beyond counting: every head is in some sense his, every pair of eyes, every step. He covered the earth on every side, and stood beyond it by ten fingers' width. Not a mountain more: ten fingers. Then verse two: purusha eva idam sarvam. The Purusha is all this, whatever has been and whatever is to be. This is one of the oldest seeds of a teaching Hindus carry everywhere: the divine isn't somewhere else, behind the sky. It's here, in all this. The Upanishads say it again later, sarvam khalv idam brahma, all this is Brahman. And many Hindus explain their everyday greeting the same way: the folded hands of namaste bow to the divine in the person in front of you. So that rooftop crowd isn't a mass of strangers. On the hymn's picture, every face in it is one of the thousand. Next time you're squeezed into a crowded train or a packed school hallway, that's the Purusha Sukta's view: one sacred person, looking out through all those eyes. And still, ten fingers more.
screen: `PURUSHA: A PERSON.` · `A THOUSAND HEADS, EYES AND FEET.` · `PURUSHA EVA IDAM SARVAM: ALL THIS.` · `NAMASTE: BOWING TO THE DIVINE IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind three faces you'll see today: someone you love, someone you pass without noticing, someone who's hard for you. Fold your hands at your chest, and for each one, bow a little, inwardly, the way namaste does. If you pray, see the divine looking out through their eyes; if you don't, simply wish each of them well.
The Purusha Sukta. The hymn of the cosmic person: a thousand heads, eyes and feet, all that has been and will be, and still ten fingers more.
Your line: God is in all this, every face included. A thousand heads, and still ten fingers more. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting; its 'the Purusha is all this' is one root of the Hindu teaching that the divine is present in everything, which many Hindus connect with namaste.

notes: First Purusha Sukta day (1256–1261): verses 1–2. Following days take verses 3–4, 6–10, 11–12, 13–14 and 15–16.

Sanskrit given from memory in simplified transliteration: 1a sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ sahasrākṣaḥ sahasrapāt; 1d atyatiṣṭhad daśāṅgulam; 2a puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam (written open as purusha eva idam sarvam for reading). Confirm.
'About the width of two hands laid side by side' is the writer's gloss on daśāṅgulam; some read it as an idiom for 'beyond'. Confirm or cut.
'Some readers hear thousand as a way of saying beyond counting': offered as a reading, not the text's claim; confirm.
'Recited in worship and quoted by teachers from very different schools': general; confirm or soften. No claim is made about its place in any particular ritual.
The Yoga Sutras link refers back to the year-four Yoga Sutra days (purusha as seer, 4.18).
